name: The Humane League: corporate cage-free campaigns (charityevals)
summary: The Humane League (US) wins and enforces corporate cage-free egg commitments in the US and, through the Open Wing Alliance it coordinates and funds, worldwide. This model counts its 2025 spending (all programs except US legislative and legal policy work, broiler campaigns and THL UK's policy and fish work, from the audited 2025 accounts) against the hens under the commitments it and the alliance won in 2025 and under the existing pledges it held 131 companies to: about 1.4 years of healthy life per $1,000 at the defaults, a little over half of it from accountability work, which is credited with its share of the 7.5 million hens THL counts as leaving cages in 2025. The biggest uncertainties are how much of companies' compliance a year of pressure actually causes (a judgment) and how many hens the alliance's 212 other new policies cover; with the shared values at their defaults the plausible range still spans about two hundredfold. The result is below the median of its peers because THL's own pace of hens leaving cages (7.5 million a year against 162.5 million under pressed pledges) means each year of pressure moves only a small share of the stock.

sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

sections.title: In chicken pain days
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for every animal model. The shared SAD figures are Ambitious Impact's, which count each species' pain as a share of a person's with its own species weights. Here those weights come out and Rethink Priorities' go in, so every species is counted in days of a chicken's disabling pain. How a chicken compares with a person is the one animal slider.

rows.label: Share of 2025 program spending on US legislative and legal policy work (not modelled)
rows.explainer: THL's annual report splits 2025 program spending into Global Programs 36% (incl. the $2.15m grant to THL UK), Education & Mobilization 33%, US Public Policy & Corporate Engagement 17% and OWA & APA grants 14%. All of it serves corporate cage-free and broiler campaigns except the legislative and legal work (Animal Policy Alliance, defending Proposition 12 and Question 3, opposing the EATS Act). Anchor: the 2025 Form 990 Schedule C reports $406,653 of lobbying (grassroots $159,162, direct $247,491) and the 990 $300k of APA grants; with policy staff time on litigation and coalition work that is about $1.1m of $14.6m, 7.5%. Low 5% (lobbying and grants only), high 11% (half of the 'US Public Policy & Corporate Engagement' line plus APA grants). Below a tenth of program spending, so it is left out of both cost and benefit (What isn't modelled).

rows.label: Share of 2025 program spending on broiler (meat chicken) campaigns (not modelled)
rows.explainer: Broiler work (Better Chicken Commitment and European Chicken Commitment campaigns) has no published bird counts for 2025, so its cost is taken out with its benefit. Anchor: the $2.15m grant to THL UK is 14.7% of program spending (audited statements, note 7); THL UK's public work is split between broiler welfare (the Better Chicken Commitment, its legal challenge on fast-growing breeds) cage-free accountability on UK companies, and UK cage-ban lobbying and fish work (uk_other_share_of_programs); about half of it is broiler work, 7%; the alliance's 18 broiler policies of its 234 add about 1% of the OWA grants and staff. Best 8%; low 4% (THL UK mostly cage-free accountability, which the accountability branch counts), high 13% (THL UK almost all broiler work, plus US broiler campaigns). Below a tenth of program spending, so left out (What isn't modelled).

rows.label: Share of 2025 program spending on THL UK's policy and fish work (not modelled)
rows.explainer: THL UK, funded by THL's $2.15m grant (14.7% of program spending), also lobbies for a UK ban on cages and campaigns on farmed fish, besides its broiler and cage-free corporate work. Neither has outcome counts for 2025. Best a fifth of the grant, 3% of program spending; low 1%, high 5%. Under a tenth, left out with its benefit.

rows.label: Spending on corporate cage-free campaigns, accountability and the Open Wing Alliance, 2025
rows.explainer: All 2025 program spending except the US legislative and legal policy work, the broiler campaigns and THL UK's policy and fish work: corporate negotiations and pressure campaigns, the Education & Mobilization team that runs them (changemakers, investigations, communications), Global Programs including the cage-free part of the grant to THL UK, and Open Wing Alliance grants. Convention 1: program expenses times the modelled share.

rows.label: Hens per year per other alliance cage-free policy
rows.explainer: No hen count is published for the alliance's 2025 policies. Many are small companies (more than 60 in Africa; restaurants and hotels in Indonesia), a few are large (Agro Innova, Ghana, about 15 million eggs a month, about 600,000 hens). THL's own four 2025 wins average 400,000 hens each, which bounds the mean from above for the rest. Best guess 10,000 hens a policy (a mean pulled up by a few producers and retailers); low 2,000 (all small caterers), high 50,000 (several national retailers among them).

rows.explainer: Hens per year in the supply chains of the 131 companies THL pressed in 2025 to keep earlier cage-free pledges (Subway, Ahold Delhaize, Best Western, Walmart, REWE, Compass Group and others), THL's own count ('more than 160M' in the CEO letter and the 990). rows.label: New commitments: share of hens not yet cage-free when the commitment was made
rows.explainer: A new commitment is made by a company still buying caged eggs; some already source part of their eggs cage-free. Best 90%, 70% to 100%.

rows.label: Alliance policies: share of hens not yet cage-free when the policy was made
rows.explainer: The alliance's new policies are, like THL's own, made by companies still buying caged eggs, many in Africa and Asia where cage-free supply is scarce, so few are already part-way. Best 90%; low 70% (some already source partly cage-free), high 100%.

rows.label: Accountability: share of the hens not yet cage-free during the 2025 campaigns
rows.explainer: THL describes the 162.5 million as hens 'to spare ... more every year', on top of the 7.5 million it counts as spared in 2025: mostly hens still caged. Some targets were already part-way (REWE 83%, Best Western about 70%, OWA review), but THL's figure is the hens still to be spared, so best 95%, 80% to 100%.

rows.label: Share of the hens in enriched (furnished) cages rather than battery cages
rows.explainer: Battery cages are banned in the EU and UK, so hens of European targets (REWE, about 7 million hens; Lidl; Brakes) move from enriched cages; hens in the US, Latin America, Asia and Africa (Subway, Ahold Delhaize, Walmart, the alliance's African and Asian policies) move from battery cages. Most of the 162.5 million are in US and global chains, so best 20%; low 5% (almost all US), high 40%.

rows.label: SADs averted per hen-year out of cages
rows.explainer: The shared figures for the two changes (facts/sad_factors.json): a battery-caged hen moved to an aviary (2024 SADs) and an enriched-caged hen moved to an aviary (2025 SADs), weighted by the share of hens in each. The species section splits them back by version.

rows.label: Share of the SADs from battery-cage hens (2024 SAD version)
rows.explainer: Used only to split the SADs by SAD version in the species section.

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer to how many years a won pledge, law or rule counts before it would have come anyway (Your values → How impact is counted; docs/normalization.md 2.9). Never the charity's or an evaluator's own figure. It applies to accountability too: a pledge kept because of pressure counts the same years as one won.

rows.label: New commitments: years from the win until the commitments take effect
rows.explainer: New cage-free commitments are usually given a deadline two to five years out (Heron Foods, published 2025, by July 2026; producer commitments in Ghana and Indonesia typically by 2028-2030). Best 3 years, 1 to 6.

rows.label: Alliance policies: years from the win until the policies take effect
rows.explainer: The alliance's 2025 policies carry deadlines like THL's own: a few immediate (restaurants that switch on committing), most two to five years out for producers and retailers in Africa, Asia and Latin America. Best 3 years; low 1, high 6.

rows.label: Accountability: years from the pressure until the changes take effect
rows.explainer: From the pressure to the hens actually leaving cages. At THL's own 2025 pace (7.5 million hens spared against about 119 million still to come under pressed pledges that will be kept) the pressed stock takes about 14-16 years to clear (acc_years_of_pressure), so the hens a year's pressure moves leave cages on average about halfway through: best 7 years. Low 2 (pressure moves the pledges that are nearly due, such as Subway's US supply, switched by November 2025), high 10.

rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit.

rows.explainer: For reading only: each branch discounts its own wait.

rows.label: Discount for the wait (hen-weighted average of the branches)

rows.explainer: For reading only: each branch applies its own.

rows.explainer: For reading only: each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment: how far to trust THL's count of hens under its new commitments
rows.explainer: The SADs per hen-year, pledges kept and years counted are shared figures with their own ranges, so this covers only what is THL's: the 1.6 million hens under its four new commitments are THL's own count, unverified by a tracker, and the four companies are not named. Applied to THL's own new commitments; the accountability branch has its own (acc_evidence_adj, on the count of hens spared that it rests on) and the alliance branch none, its hen count being our own judgment. Anchor: the template's 0.7 for unverified reach; THL does not name its four new commitments, so nothing lifts it above that. Low 0.5 (the count covers whole groups of which only part committed), high 1.

rows.label: New commitments: share that would not have been made in 2025 without the campaign
rows.explainer: How long the change would take to come anyway is the shared years counted, so this is only the chance a company would have committed this year unprompted. Most new commitments follow a campaign or a negotiation with a deadline; best 90%, 70-100%.

rows.label: Alliance policies: share that would not have been made in 2025 without the campaigns
rows.explainer: The member groups' campaigns, often in markets with no prior cage-free pressure (more than 60 policies in Africa), are the reason these companies commit this year; the shared years counted already cover how soon the change would have come anyway. Best 90%; low 70% (some companies were already planning a policy), high 100%.

rows.label: Accountability: share of pressed pledges that would never be kept without the pressure
rows.explainer: The share of the compliance of pledges THL presses that would not happen at all (within the years a won reform counts) without accountability work. Accelerating a pledge that would be kept anyway counts zero here: how long a change takes to come anyway is the shared years counted, not this row. Anchor, the companies THL names as pressed in 2025: three were stalled or silent for years (Walmart, four years of silence; Best Western, silent on a 2025 deadline; Ahold Delhaize, the slowest sector) and three were on track or early (Subway ahead of its deadline, Cheesecake Factory six years early, Compass Group reporting). If about half of the stalled ones would never have complied unpressed, about a quarter to a third of pressed compliance is owed to pressure. Half the named cases on track or early, and most pledges kept across trackers, keep the share well below a half. Best 30%; low 10% (most stalled companies would comply eventually anyway), high 60% (most stalled companies would default).

rows.label: Hens THL counts as spared from cages worldwide in 2025

source.title: The Humane League, 2025 Annual Report
source.quote: 7.5M HENS SPARED from cages around the globe, with additional commitments cemented TO SPARE 162.5M MORE EVERY YEAR

rows.explainer: THL's own count of hens that left cages in 2025 under the commitments it works on: the pace at which the pressed stock is being kept.

rows.label: Accountability: how far to trust THL's count of hens spared in 2025
rows.explainer: The accountability branch reduces to THL's 7.5 million hens spared in 2025 (the 162.5 million, the not-yet-compliant share and the shared rate of pledges kept cancel out), so this is the discount on that one count. It is THL's own, unverified, and loosely defined: hens of companies reporting progress, possibly including partial progress and companies outside the 131 pressed. A previous year's THL estimate was about 3.4 million hens spared (Fair and Fowl report, as summarised on a THL staff member's EA Forum profile, https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/users/cara-schwalbach-thl), so the count more than doubled in a year. Best 0.7, the template's figure for unverified reach; low 0.45 (half the 7.5 million is partial or unpressed progress), high 1.

rows.label: Accountability: years a pledge is pressed until it is kept
rows.explainer: THL presses the same companies year after year until they comply, so one year's pressure is credited with its share of the cumulative effect, not all of it (Convention 3, flows not stocks). The years follow from THL's own pace: the hens still caged under pressed pledges that will be kept (not-yet-compliant hens times the shared rate of pledges kept) divided by the hens THL counts as spared in 2025. About 16 years at the defaults; its range comes from the inputs'.

rows.label: Accountability: share of the compliance owed to the 2025 pressure
rows.explainer: The cumulative share owed to pressure, spread over the years a pledge is pressed: 2025's share of it.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway (outcome-weighted average of the branches)
rows.formula: (new_hen_years * new_counterfactual_adj + owa_hen_years * owa_counterfactual_adj + acc_hen_years * acc_counterfactual_adj) / hen_years_total
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches (weighted by discounted hen-years before adjustments), for reading only and not applied itself (Convention 4): each branch applies its own counterfactual.

rows.label: Share of pledged hens whose pledge is later pressed by accountability campaigns
rows.explainer: Only pledges that fall behind get pressed. THL pressed 131 companies covering more than 160 million hens in 2025, a large part of all hens under pledges it tracks, and laggards are concentrated among the biggest buyers that hold most hens. Best 70%; low 50%, high 100%.

rows.label: Share of a new pledge's compliance that comes without later accountability pressure
rows.explainer: Of the pledges kept that a new commitment is credited with, the part owed to later pressure (on the pledges that get pressed) is credited to the accountability work of later years (as this year's accountability branch credits pressure on earlier pledges), so the new-commitment branches count only the rest.

rows.label: New commitments: THL's share of the resources behind them
rows.explainer: THL's share of the resources behind its four 2025 commitments. THL counts these as its own, but they were won in markets where alliance members campaign too: the alliance review names grant-funded member campaigns behind the year's new producer commitment in Ghana (Agro Innova) and new commitments in Indonesia, and THL's own method credits itself with half of each commitment it works on ('we went with 50% as a conservative estimate', thehumaneleague.org/article/fifty-cents-to-spare-a-hen). THL does not name its four, and the year's named producer and Indonesian wins are alliance members' grant-funded campaigns, so some of THL's four were probably won with members. Half is our best guess for that mix, not a conservative case: THL's negotiators and funding on one side, the members' local campaigns on the other. Low 30% (members did most of the work), high 80% (THL ran them alone).

rows.label: Alliance policies: THL's share of the resources behind them
rows.explainer: The member groups win these policies; THL trains, coordinates and part-funds them. Anchor: THL's 2025 OWA grants were $2.11m to 36 groups and its OWA team perhaps $1-1.5m, against more than 525 member staff working on cage-free and broiler campaigns (OWA 2025 review; at $20-30k a staff year in the countries concerned, $10-16m). THL's share about 20%; 10-40%.

rows.label: Accountability: THL's share of the resources behind the pressure
rows.explainer: THL's share of everyone's spending on pressing these companies. THL: most of its $11.9m of modelled 2025 program spending goes to accountability (Education & Mobilization's $4.7m of changemakers, investigations and communications, the corporate engagement team, the cage-free part of Global Programs), about $8m. Partners on the same targets: Animal Equality (Ahold Delhaize), Mercy For Animals and other US groups, and the alliance members who campaigned on Best Western, REWE and the egg investigation (37 countries), part of the alliance's more than 525 campaign staff (OWA review), plausibly $8-15m. THL's share about 40%; low 25% (partners' spending at the high end), high 60% (THL alone on most US targets).

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome (outcome-weighted average of the branches)
rows.formula: (new_hen_years * new_attribution_share_shared + owa_hen_years * owa_attribution_share_shared + acc_hen_years * acc_attribution_share_shared) / hen_years_total
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches (weighted by discounted hen-years before adjustments), for reading only and not applied itself (Convention 4): each branch applies its own share.
